column2: Repeat every value twice before moving to the next value.~That interleaves copies: [1,2] becomes [1,1,2,2] instead of two complete copies.
column3: Append a reversed copy after the original.~The second half must preserve the original order too.
column4: Double each value and keep the original length.~Concatenation changes the number of elements, not their numeric values.

column2: Compare only neighboring numbers in the original order.~Equal values can be separated, as in [1,2,1].
column3: Insert each number into the set, then check whether it is present.~Every newly inserted number is present, including the first occurrence.
column4: Count negative and positive values separately and compare those totals.~Signs do not identify whether the same value occurs twice.

column2: Compare only the sets of characters.~Sets lose multiplicities; 'aab' and 'abb' use the same letters but are not anagrams.
column3: Require the characters to match at every position.~Anagrams may rearrange characters, so positions need not match.
column4: Compare string lengths and the sums of character codes.~Different character multisets can have equal lengths and equal code sums.

column2: Insert the current number before looking up its complement.~This can pair an element with itself when twice its value equals the target.
column3: Sort values and return the matching positions in the sorted array.~The required indices belong to the original input; sorting without retaining them loses that information.
column4: Find two matching values and return those values.~The result must contain indices, not the values themselves.

column2: Return the longest substring shared anywhere in every string.~A prefix must begin at position zero in every string.
column3: Compare only the first and second strings.~A later string may disagree or end earlier.
column4: Stop only when characters differ, ignoring a shorter string's end.~A valid common prefix cannot extend past any input string.

column2: Group words only by their length.~Equal length does not imply equal character counts.
column3: Group words by their distinct character sets.~Repeated-letter counts distinguish groups such as 'abb' and 'aab'.
column4: Sort each group's output but return only one word per key.~The output must preserve every original word, including duplicates.

column2: Delete matching values while always advancing the same scan index.~Deleting shifts the next value into the current position, which can skip consecutive matches.
column3: Count retained values but leave the array unchanged.~The judge also reads the retained values from the first k array positions.
column4: Advance the write position for every scanned value.~Then matching values leave gaps in the retained prefix.

column2: Keep the number with the greatest numeric value.~Magnitude and frequency are unrelated.
column3: Switch candidates whenever the next number differs.~A single disagreement does not cancel all prior support for a candidate.
column4: Increase the balance for every value and never decrease it.~Cancellation requires competing values to reduce the current candidate's balance.

column2: Use one stored key per hash bucket and overwrite collisions.~Different keys can have the same remainder and must coexist in that bucket.
column3: Treat a nonempty bucket as proof that the queried key exists.~A collision is not key equality; the actual keys must be checked.
column4: Clear an entire bucket when removing one key.~That also removes unrelated colliding keys.

column2: Store values by hash remainder without retaining full keys.~Colliding keys would overwrite one another and queries could return the wrong value.
column3: Always append a new pair when an existing key is updated.~A later get could encounter the stale pair instead of the new value.
column4: Remove the first pair from the selected bucket.~The matching full key may occur later among colliding entries.

column2: Build a max-heap and return its internal array immediately.~A heap orders parents above children, not every adjacent pair.
column3: Extract the root but restore the heap across the entire array.~That disturbs the suffix whose maximum values were already placed.
column4: Use a min-heap while moving its root to the final free position.~This puts the smallest values at the end and produces the wrong direction.

column2: Move the middle position forward after every swap with the high end.~The incoming value from the high end has not been classified yet.
column3: Treat every value except zero as a two.~Ones need their own middle region.
column4: Stop when the middle position equals the high position.~That final unknown position still needs classification.

column2: Return the k largest numeric values.~The ranking is by occurrence count, not numeric magnitude.
column3: Collect buckets from the lowest frequency upward.~That selects the least frequent values first.
column4: Place every occurrence into the output buckets separately.~Each distinct value should be selected once, using its total frequency.

column2: Join strings with a separator and split on that separator.~Input strings may contain the separator, so boundaries become ambiguous.
column3: Prefix a length but read only one digit of it.~Strings of length ten or greater require multi-digit lengths.
column4: Drop empty strings while encoding.~Decoding must reproduce empty elements and their positions too.

column2: Add the top and left prefix sums without subtracting their overlap.~The overlapping upper-left rectangle would be counted twice.
column3: Answer a rectangle using only its bottom-right prefix value.~That prefix also includes cells above and left of the requested rectangle.
column4: Subtract the top and left strips without adding their shared corner back.~Their overlap is removed twice and must be restored once.

column2: Multiply all values and divide by the current value.~Zero values break division, and the selected approach intentionally avoids division.
column3: Store products that include the current value in both passes.~The current value must be excluded, not multiplied twice.
column4: Use only the running product from the left.~The result also needs every value strictly to the right.

column2: Keep one global set of all digits on the board.~A digit may validly occur in different rows, columns, and boxes.
column3: Check rows and columns but ignore boxes.~A repeated digit inside a box can avoid sharing a row or column.
column4: Count empty cells as repeated digits.~Dots represent missing values and must not participate in duplicate checks.

column2: Count increasing runs only in the given array order.~Consecutive values need not be adjacent in the original order.
column3: Extend runs from every occurrence and count duplicates as extra length.~A consecutive sequence contains distinct integer steps, not repeated copies.
column4: Return the difference between the minimum and maximum values plus one.~Missing intermediate values can split that range into separate runs.

column2: Take only the single best buy-sell pair.~This problem allows multiple profitable transactions.
column3: Add every adjacent difference, including negative ones.~Losing overnight positions can be avoided; only positive rises should contribute.
column4: Sort prices before adding rises.~Sorting destroys the chronological buy-before-sell constraint.

column2: Use only one candidate balance.~There may be two values occurring more than n/3 times.
column3: Return the two surviving candidates without recounting.~Cancellation identifies possibilities; it does not prove either exceeds the threshold.
column4: Keep values occurring exactly n/3 times.~The required frequency is strictly greater than n/3.

column2: Use a set of earlier prefix sums without counts.~Several identical prefixes can each form a different valid subarray.
column3: Record the current prefix before counting matches.~For k=0 this counts an empty subarray ending at the same prefix.
column4: Use a shrinking positive-sum window for every input.~Negative numbers break the monotonic sum behavior that such a window requires.

column2: Use each value directly as its destination index.~Value v belongs at v-1, and values outside 1 through n are not valid destinations.
column3: Keep swapping even when the destination already holds the same value.~Duplicate values can cause an endless swap loop.
column4: Return n whenever all positions are filled correctly.~If 1 through n are present, the missing positive is n+1.

column2: Swap every position with its mirror while scanning the whole array.~Each pair is swapped twice, restoring the original string.
column3: Move both positions toward the right after a swap.~The boundaries must converge inward to visit opposite pairs.
column4: Build a reversed string and leave the input array unchanged.~The required operation mutates the supplied character array.

column2: Compare every character exactly as written.~The statement ignores punctuation and letter case.
column3: Skip punctuation only at the left boundary.~Punctuation on the right also needs to be skipped.
column4: Accept the string as soon as its outer characters match.~All remaining inward pairs must match too.

column2: Always remove the left character at the first mismatch.~Sometimes only removing the right character yields a palindrome.
column3: Remove both mismatching characters and continue.~That spends two deletions when at most one is allowed.
column4: Allow another deletion every time a later mismatch occurs.~After the first deletion choice, the remaining interval must already be a palindrome.

column2: Append both strings completely, one after the other.~The required merge alternates their characters while both have characters.
column3: Stop when either string ends.~The longer string's remaining characters must still be appended.
column4: Append the second string's character before the first at each position.~The required alternating order starts with the first string.

column2: Merge forward directly into nums1 without saving unread values.~An early write can overwrite a nums1 value that still needs comparison.
column3: Compare the unused capacity zeros as real input values.~Only nums1's first m positions are input values.
column4: Stop as soon as nums1's original values are exhausted.~Remaining nums2 values still must be copied into nums1.

column2: Remove only one occurrence of every repeated value.~A value may appear many times; only one occurrence belongs in the output prefix.
column3: Use a set to count distinct values without rewriting the prefix.~The result contract also requires the first k positions to hold the unique values.
column4: Advance the write position whenever the next value is equal.~The write position advances only for a newly encountered distinct value.

column2: Move the right pointer left when the sum is too small.~That can only reduce the sum further in this sorted array.
column3: Allow both pointers to select the same position.~The two values must come from different positions.
column4: Return zero-based positions.~This problem explicitly requires one-based indices.

column2: Return the first matching triplet and stop.~The task requests every unique zero-sum triplet.
column3: Run the inward search without first sorting.~The pointer movement rule depends on sorted order.
column4: Record every matching index triple without skipping equal choices.~Different index triples can represent the same value triplet.

column2: Fix two values, then let the remaining pointers reuse either fixed index.~All four positions must be distinct.
column3: Compare the four-value sum with zero rather than the supplied target.~Unlike 3Sum, the required sum is an arbitrary target.
column4: Skip duplicates only for the first fixed value.~Duplicates in the second choice or moving pair can still repeat quadruplets.

column2: Reverse only the whole array.~A full reversal changes the order within both rotated segments.
column3: Use k directly even when it exceeds the array length.~Rotation repeats every n positions, so k must be reduced modulo n.
column4: Reverse the first k values and stop.~The full array and remaining segment are also needed for this three-reversal plan.

column2: Move the taller boundary after measuring each container.~Keeping the shorter limit while reducing width cannot improve the current container.
column3: Compute area using the taller height.~Water escapes over the shorter boundary, which limits the usable height.
column4: Choose the two tallest lines without considering their distance.~The area also depends on the width between the lines.

column2: Always put the two heaviest people together.~They may exceed the weight limit even when each can pair with someone lighter.
column3: Count two boats whenever the lightest and heaviest do not fit together.~Only the heaviest must be assigned alone at that step; the lightest may pair later.
column4: Ignore the final person when the pointers meet.~A remaining unpaired person still needs one boat.

column2: Use only the highest bar on the left to determine water.~A lower right boundary may let that proposed water escape.
column3: Count water as the difference between neighboring bars.~Trapped water depends on bounding maxima, which may be far away.
column4: Process the side with the larger maximum as if that maximum alone bounded water.~The smaller side provides the currently justified limiting boundary.

column2: Keep every earlier value forever.~Equal values farther than k positions apart do not satisfy the distance constraint.
column3: Check only the immediately previous value.~A valid duplicate may be up to k positions away.
column4: Insert the current value before checking membership.~That falsely matches the current position with itself.

column2: Subtract the global minimum from the global maximum without checking their order.~The maximum price may occur before the minimum price.
column3: Add every positive daily rise.~That can combine multiple transactions, but only one buy-sell pair is allowed.
column4: Always buy on the first day.~A cheaper purchase day may appear later before the best sale.

column2: Remove only one left character when a duplicate arrives.~The previous copy may remain inside the window after one removal.
column3: Reset the whole window after every duplicate.~A valid suffix of the old window can still contribute to the longest result.
column4: Count distinct characters in the entire string.~The requested characters must form one contiguous substring.

column2: Allow a window whenever it contains at most k distinct characters.~Replacements count positions, not distinct letter types.
column3: Replace only adjacent unequal character pairs.~The best target letter is determined by frequency across the full window.
column4: Use the total frequency in the entire string to validate every window.~Characters outside a window cannot reduce its required replacements.

column2: Compare the sets of letters in the window and s1.~Permutations require equal multiplicities, not just matching distinct letters.
column3: Let the comparison window grow without removing old characters.~A matching permutation has exactly len(s1) characters.
column4: Check only whether s1 occurs in its original order.~Any rearrangement of s1 may be the matching substring.

column2: Shrink only once after the sum reaches the target.~Further shrinking may preserve validity and produce a shorter answer.
column3: Return the first valid window length.~A later window may reach the target with fewer elements.
column4: Sort values before choosing a short group.~The chosen values must be contiguous in the original order.

column2: On equal boundary distances, prefer the window farther right.~Ties favor smaller values, so the left window wins.
column3: Search all n start positions for a k-element slice.~Only starts through n-k leave enough elements in the array.
column4: Return the k values in order of distance from x.~The output must be sorted by value, as the chosen contiguous slice already is.

column2: Check only whether every distinct target character appears.~Repeated target characters impose additional count requirements.
column3: Stop at the first window covering the target.~That window may still shrink, and later windows may be shorter.
column4: Shrink the window even after a required count drops below its target.~Further shrinking cannot preserve coverage until the right side expands again.

column2: Keep candidate values but discard their positions.~The algorithm needs indices to expire values that have left the window.
column3: Remove smaller candidates from the front only.~Dominated candidates are removed from the back; the front holds the maximum.
column4: Emit a maximum before the first k elements have arrived.~Those prefixes are shorter than the required full window.

column2: Keep only the running total and discard individual scores.~Doubling, addition, and cancellation need the most recent valid score values.
column3: For cancellation, append a zero score.~Cancellation removes the last valid score, changing which scores later operations refer to.
column4: Apply plus to the last two operation strings.~Those operations may not be numeric scores; use the last two valid scores instead.

column2: Compare total counts of opening and closing brackets.~Counts do not enforce nesting order or bracket type.
column3: Match a closer with the oldest unmatched opener.~Nested brackets close in last-in-first-out order.
column4: Return true after processing all characters even if openers remain.~Unclosed opening brackets make the string invalid.

column2: Append every new value to the active queue's back and pop its front.~That remains FIFO rather than the required stack order.
column3: Transfer active values before enqueueing the new value into the helper.~The new value needs to end up at the front to become the next pop.
column4: Copy values into the helper without emptying the active queue.~The queues must exchange roles cleanly; old contents cannot remain duplicated.

column2: Pop directly from the input stack whenever it is nonempty.~That returns the newest queued value before older values.
column3: Transfer all inputs onto a nonempty output stack before every pop.~Newer inputs would sit above older queued values and break FIFO order.
column4: Declare the queue empty whenever either stack is empty.~The queue is empty only when both stacks contain no values.

column2: Remember only the smallest value ever pushed.~After that value is popped, an earlier minimum may need to be restored.
column3: Pop values but leave the minimum stack unchanged.~The two stacks would describe different logical depths.
column4: Store each minimum only once, ignoring repeated equal minima.~Popping one duplicate minimum must not erase the remaining equal minimum.

column2: Apply operators in ordinary infix precedence order.~Reverse Polish notation determines operands directly through the stack order.
column3: Treat the first popped value as the left operand.~Subtraction and division require the second popped value on the left.
column4: Round division down toward negative infinity.~The required integer division truncates toward zero.

column2: Collide every pair of neighboring asteroids with opposite signs.~A left-moving asteroid before a right-moving one is moving away, not toward it.
column3: Resolve at most one collision per incoming asteroid.~A large incoming asteroid can destroy several earlier survivors.
column4: Let one asteroid survive when equal sizes collide.~Equal-size opposing asteroids both disappear.

column2: Resolve earlier days when the new temperature is equal.~The requested day must be strictly warmer.
column3: Store temperatures only and return their numeric difference.~The answer is an index distance in days, so positions must be retained.
column4: Compare each day only with the next day.~Its first warmer day can be much farther in the future.

column2: Pop only strictly lower prices.~The span also includes earlier prices equal to today's price.
column3: Add one for each popped stack entry.~Each entry can represent many collapsed days through its stored span.
column4: Count every earlier lower price, even across a higher price.~The span must be consecutive and stops at the first greater price.

column2: Process cars from farthest to nearest and use the same arrival comparison.~The merge decision needs the already known fleet ahead of each car.
column3: Count a new fleet when arrival times are equal.~Those cars meet by the target and belong to the same fleet.
column4: Group cars by equal speed alone.~Different speeds can still merge because starting positions differ.

column2: Treat every component containing a dot as a parent step.~Only the exact component '..' moves to the parent; names like '...' are valid.
column3: Keep parent steps when already at the root.~An absolute path cannot move above the root.
column4: Remove every slash before processing the path.~Slashes separate components and preserve the directory boundaries.

column2: Use one repetition count for all nested brackets.~Each nested level needs its own saved count and outer text.
column3: Repeat only the final character when a bracket closes.~The count applies to the complete decoded text inside that bracket.
column4: Read only one digit for a repetition count.~Counts can have multiple digits and must be accumulated in base ten.

column2: Always pop the most recently pushed value.~Frequency takes priority; recency breaks ties only among maximum-frequency values.
column3: Keep just one value for each frequency.~Several values can share that frequency and need recency ordering.
column4: Decrease the maximum frequency after every pop.~It should decrease only when that frequency's stack becomes empty.

column2: Use each bar's height multiplied by the full array length.~A shorter intervening bar limits how far that height can extend.
column3: Resolve a popped height using only its immediate neighboring index.~Its valid rectangle can span many bars up to the nearest shorter boundary.
column4: Finish without flushing unresolved heights.~An increasing suffix may contain the best rectangle and still needs evaluation.

column2: Keep the checked middle index as the lower boundary when searching right.~With an inclusive interval this can prevent progress in a small range.
column3: Choose a half before comparing its middle value with the target.~Discarding a half requires the comparison result to justify it.
column4: Stop when one candidate remains and return minus one.~That last value may be the target and still needs checking.

column2: Return minus one whenever no equal value is found.~The task requires the valid insertion position even when the target is absent.
column3: Find the first value strictly greater than the target.~An existing equal value should be its insertion position.
column4: Exclude position n from the candidate range.~A target larger than every element must be inserted at the end.

column2: Interpret a negative guess response as a request to search higher.~A negative response means the guessed value is above the hidden number.
column3: Search from zero through n minus one.~The allowed hidden-number range is 1 through n.
column4: Return the middle guess after its first nonzero response.~That response only eliminates a half; it has not identified the number.

column2: Return the first integer whose square exceeds x.~That is one above the floor square root.
column3: Search only for an integer whose square equals x.~Many inputs are not perfect squares but still have a floor square root.
column4: Round the ordinary square root to the nearest integer.~Rounding up can exceed the required floor.

column2: Search each row as if all rows shared the same column index.~The global midpoint maps through division and remainder by the column count.
column3: Apply binary search to rows only and compare their first elements.~The target may occur later inside the candidate row.
column4: Treat a flattened index as both its row and column.~A flat position needs separate row and column coordinates.

column2: Divide the total number of bananas by h and round once.~Time is rounded up separately for every pile because an hour serves only one pile.
column3: Choose the largest speed that meets the deadline.~The question asks for the smallest feasible speed.
column4: Combine leftover fractions of hours across different piles.~A partially used hour cannot be shared between piles in this problem.

column2: Sort packages by weight before checking a capacity.~Packages must be shipped in the original order.
column3: Use average daily weight as a guaranteed feasible capacity.~A single heavy package or an ordered boundary may require more capacity.
column4: Search below the heaviest package's weight.~Every package must fit intact on the ship.

column2: Discard the middle whenever its value is below the right endpoint.~That middle may itself be the minimum and must remain a candidate.
column3: Compare values as though the entire array were unrotated.~Rotation breaks global order; the middle-to-right comparison identifies the correct side.
column4: Return the rotation index instead of the value there.~The required output is the minimum value.

column2: Use ordinary sorted-array comparisons across the entire rotated range.~A rotation can put larger values before smaller ones, invalidating that elimination rule.
column3: Always keep the half that is sorted.~The target may lie in the other half; its bounds must be checked.
column4: Return the first smaller-than-target position.~The task requires an exact value match and its original position.

column2: Assume equal left and middle values reveal which half is sorted.~Duplicates can hide the rotation, requiring cautious boundary reduction.
column3: Skip every value equal to the target before comparing.~A target match is already a valid answer and must not be discarded.
column4: Return an index instead of a boolean.~This version asks only whether the target exists.

column2: Return the most recently stored value regardless of query time.~A query cannot use a value recorded after its timestamp.
column3: Require an exact timestamp match.~The latest earlier timestamp is also valid.
column4: Search all keys' timestamp histories as one list.~Each query belongs to one key's own ordered values.

column2: Partition values after sorting them by size.~Subarrays must stay contiguous in the original order.
column3: Always split into groups of equal element count.~Equal lengths do not minimize the largest sum when values differ.
column4: Accept a bound even when one element exceeds it.~Every element must fit inside some group's maximum-sum bound.

column2: Average the separate medians of the two arrays.~Different lengths and interleaving values make that average unreliable.
column3: Partition both arrays at the same index.~Their partitions must contain the required combined count, not equal local counts.
column4: Validate only one cross-boundary inequality.~Both arrays' left values must be no larger than both right values.

column2: Binary-search the entire mountain using only increasing-order comparisons.~The descending side has the opposite order.
column3: Search the descending side first and return its match immediately.~A smaller matching index may exist on the increasing side.
column4: Find the peak and return it for every target.~The peak is only a boundary; the target still requires a value search.

column2: Reverse the current link before saving the original next node.~That loses the link needed to continue through the unreversed remainder.
column3: Reverse node values while leaving links unchanged.~This guided solution reverses the links and returns the resulting head.
column4: Return the original head after reversing every link.~The original head becomes the tail; the previous pointer holds the new head.

column2: Alternate nodes from the two lists regardless of value.~The merged output must remain sorted.
column3: Stop and discard the other list when either input ends.~The unconsumed sorted remainder belongs at the output tail.
column4: Return the dummy node as part of the merged list.~The dummy is only an anchor; output begins at its next link.

column2: Declare a cycle when two nodes have equal values.~Different nodes may store equal values; a cycle depends on node identity.
column3: Move both pointers one step at the same time from the same start.~They remain together even in an acyclic list, so a meeting proves nothing.
column4: Advance the fast pointer twice without checking its next link.~A finite list may end before the second step.

column2: Reverse the entire list and return that order.~The required order alternates from the original front and back.
column3: Merge the halves before detaching their original connecting link.~The old connection can create a cycle during interleaving.
column4: Alternate with the second half in its original order.~The back half must be reversed to supply nodes from the original end inward.

column2: Move the leading pointer only n links from the dummy and use the same deletion rule.~The slower pointer must stop immediately before the removal node; this plan needs a gap of n+1.
column3: Delete the nth node counted from the front.~The requested position is measured from the end.
column4: Skip the dummy node and assume the head never changes.~Removing the original head is a valid case.

column2: Copy next links but point random links at original nodes.~A deep copy must connect only to cloned nodes.
column3: Use node values as unique keys for the clone map.~Different original nodes may share a value but require distinct clones.
column4: Create a fresh clone every time a random link is encountered.~Multiple references to one original must share the same cloned node.

column2: Stop when either input list is exhausted.~The longer number's remaining digits and any carry must still be processed.
column3: Append each raw digit sum without carrying.~Each result node must store one decimal digit.
column4: Discard the carry after both lists end.~A final carry requires an additional output node.

column2: Return the first cycle meeting value immediately.~The first meeting can occur inside the cycle away from its entry.
column3: Move through the array only by increasing indices.~The cycle model follows values as next indices, not neighboring positions.
column4: Reset both pointers to the start after the meeting.~Keeping one at the meeting lets the second phase locate the cycle entry.

column2: Reverse the entire list even when the requested interval is smaller.~Nodes outside the selected segment must preserve their order.
column3: Detach the next node without reconnecting the remainder.~The unreversed suffix would be lost.
column4: Return the original head unconditionally.~When the segment starts at position one, the list head changes.

column2: Treat equal head and rear positions as always empty.~A full circular buffer can have the same index relationship; the count distinguishes the states.
column3: Advance indices without taking modulo capacity.~Indices must wrap back into the fixed array.
column4: Overwrite the oldest item when a full queue receives an enqueue.~This interface must reject that enqueue instead.

column2: Evict the smallest key when capacity is exceeded.~Eviction is based on recency, not key order.
column3: Update recency on put but not on successful get.~Reading an existing key makes it recently used too.
column4: Remove an evicted node only from the linked list.~Its key must also be removed from the lookup map.

column2: Evict the least recently used key regardless of frequency.~Minimum frequency has priority; recency breaks only frequency ties.
column3: Increase frequency only on insertion.~Successful gets and updates also affect usage frequency.
column4: Leave min_freq unchanged after its final key is promoted.~Eviction would then look in an empty frequency bucket.

column2: Append one complete input list before moving to the next.~Values from different sorted lists may interleave.
column3: Heap-select only the initial heads and never add successors.~Most nodes would never enter the candidate pool.
column4: Choose the largest available head at every step.~The merged list must be in ascending order.

column2: Reverse the final group even when it has fewer than k nodes.~A short final group must remain unchanged.
column3: Reverse k nodes but do not reconnect the old head to the remainder.~That old head is now the group's tail and must link onward.
column4: Reverse only the node values inside each group.~This guided solution changes node links to implement the group reversal.

column2: Visit a node before descending into its left subtree.~That is preorder rather than inorder.
column3: After visiting a node, return to its left child again.~Its left subtree has already been processed; traversal continues right.
column4: Use a queue to visit nodes level by level.~That produces breadth-first order, not the selected inorder traversal.

column2: Push the left child before the right child on the LIFO stack.~The right child would then be visited first.
column3: Visit a node only after both children.~That is postorder, not preorder.
column4: Return sorted node values.~Traversal order depends on tree structure, not numeric sorting.

column2: Return the node-right-left collection without reversing it.~Postorder requires left-right-node.
column3: Push right before left and apply the same final reversal.~That reverses node-left-right into right-left-node, the wrong sibling order.
column4: Record only leaf nodes.~Postorder includes every internal node after its children too.

column2: Swap only the root's two children.~Every subtree must also be inverted.
column3: Reverse the inorder value sequence and leave links unchanged.~Inversion changes the tree's left-right structure.
column4: Replace one child with the other without saving both.~That loses one original subtree instead of swapping them.

column2: Add the depths of both children.~Depth follows one longest root-to-leaf path, not both branches together.
column3: Return one for a missing node.~An empty subtree contributes depth zero.
column4: Return the smaller child depth plus one.~That measures a shorter branch rather than the maximum depth.

column2: Return only the root's left height plus right height.~The longest path may lie entirely inside a subtree.
column3: Propagate both branches' sum as the height to the parent.~A height is one downward path, so only the taller branch can extend upward.
column4: Count the number of nodes on the diameter instead of its edges.~This problem measures diameter in edges.

column2: Check the height difference only at the root.~A deeper subtree can be unbalanced even if root heights are close.
column3: Compare subtree node counts instead of heights.~Equal sizes do not imply balanced depths.
column4: Ignore an unbalanced result from a child when parent heights match.~Every subtree must satisfy the balance condition.

column2: Compare only the multisets of stored values.~Identical values can appear in different tree structures.
column3: Treat one missing node and one present node as equal.~Corresponding missing-child positions are part of tree equality.
column4: Require just one of the two corresponding subtrees to match.~Both left and right structures must agree.

column2: Accept any node with the same value as subRoot.~The entire rooted structure and every value must match.
column3: Compare subRoot only with the main root.~The matching subtree may start deeper in the tree.
column4: Compare only the candidate subtree's leaves.~Internal nodes and missing-child positions matter too.

column2: Stop at the first node whose value equals either target's average.~An average is unrelated to the shared ancestor's position.
column3: Move left when either target is smaller.~A split across left and right means the current node is already their ancestor.
column4: Search for the deepest leaf below both target values.~The answer must be an ancestor of the actual target nodes.

column2: Attach every new value as the root's left child.~BST ordering chooses the branch and insertion must preserve existing nodes.
column3: Create the node at a missing child but ignore the recursive return value.~The parent must reconnect to the newly built subtree.
column4: Insert by tree depth alone.~The selected branch is determined by the value comparison.

column2: Remove a matching node together with all its descendants.~Its remaining values must remain in the BST.
column3: For a two-child node, copy its successor but leave the successor in place.~That duplicates a value; the original successor node must also be deleted.
column4: Replace a node with an arbitrary descendant.~The replacement must preserve all BST bounds, such as the inorder successor does.

column2: Put every visited value into one flat list.~The required output groups values by their original tree level.
column3: Keep processing until the queue is empty before closing the current level.~Newly enqueued children belong to the next level, not the current batch.
column4: Use stack order and group every two nodes together.~Level sizes vary and must follow breadth-first distance from the root.

column2: Always follow right-child links from the root.~A deeper visible node may come from a left subtree when the right subtree ends.
column3: Record the first node in a left-to-right level batch.~That gives the left-side view.
column4: Record every leaf in traversal order.~Visibility needs one rightmost node at each depth, not all leaves.

column2: Merge quadrants whenever their root values match, ignoring whether they are leaves.~An internal quadrant's root value does not prove that its cells are uniform.
column3: Split every region into only a top and a bottom half.~A quad tree uses four spatial quadrants at each subdivision.
column4: Reuse one child node for all four different quadrants.~Each quadrant represents its own grid region and may differ.

column2: Compare every node only with the global maximum in the whole tree.~Only ancestors on that node's own path can make it not good.
column3: Compare each node only with its immediate parent.~An earlier ancestor may be larger than both parent and node.
column4: Count only nodes strictly greater than every ancestor.~Equality with the path maximum still qualifies as good.

column2: Check only that each left child is smaller and each right child is larger.~A descendant can violate an older ancestor's bound.
column3: Allow a value equal to either bound.~This BST definition requires strict ordering without duplicate values.
column4: Share one narrowed bound between both recursive branches.~Left and right branches inherit different valid ranges.

column2: Visit the BST in preorder and return its kth node.~Preorder is not sorted; inorder is.
column3: Count nodes when they are pushed onto the stack, before descending left.~Inorder rank is determined when a node is popped after its left subtree, not when first discovered.
column4: Return the node object when the counter reaches k.~The requested output is that node's value.

column2: Use the inorder array's first value as every subtree root.~Preorder gives the next root; inorder gives the split boundaries.
column3: Build the right subtree before consuming the left preorder segment.~Preorder lists the left subtree before the right subtree.
column4: Split both traversals at their numeric midpoint.~Tree subtrees need not have equal sizes.

column2: Rob every node whose value is positive.~Adjacent parent-child houses cannot both be robbed.
column3: Rob a node together with each child's best unrestricted total.~Robbing the parent requires the skipped-child states specifically.
column4: Compare only taking all even depths with taking all odd depths.~The optimal combination may mix depths across different branches.

column2: Delete matching leaves only in the original tree.~Deleting children can create new matching leaves that also need removal.
column3: Delete every node whose value equals the target.~A matching internal node must stay unless it becomes a leaf.
column4: Decide whether to delete a parent before processing its children.~The decision depends on the post-deletion child structure.

column2: Return both child branches upward as one extendable path.~A path passed to the parent cannot branch in two directions at the child.
column3: Initialize the best total to zero.~All-negative trees still require a nonempty path, so zero may be invalid.
column4: Force every candidate path to include the original root.~The best path can be contained in any subtree.

column2: Serialize only non-null node values.~Without missing-child markers, different shapes can have the same value sequence.
column3: Serialize preorder but deserialize in level order.~The decoder must consume the same structural order as the encoder.
column4: Reuse the root value for missing-child tokens.~A null marker must stay distinguishable from a real value.

column2: Keep a max-heap of the largest k values and report its root.~The root would be the largest, not the kth largest of all values seen.
column3: Drop the largest retained value when the heap exceeds k.~That removes a value needed for the top-k set.
column4: Keep only k distinct values by removing duplicates.~Duplicate occurrences count toward the kth-largest position.

column2: Smash the two smallest stones each round.~The stated process selects the two heaviest remaining stones.
column3: Always insert the sum of the smashed stones.~The survivor has the absolute weight difference, or none when equal.
column4: Never reinsert the remaining difference.~That survivor must participate in later rounds.

column2: Keep the k farthest points.~The requested ranking favors smaller squared distances.
column3: Use only the x-coordinate to rank points.~Distance depends on both coordinate squares.
column4: Delete repeated point occurrences before ranking.~Each input point is a candidate occurrence; multiplicities must be preserved.

column2: Fully order only the smaller-than-pivot region regardless of target rank.~The requested rank may lie in the equal or larger region.
column3: Use k directly as the zero-based ascending rank.~Kth largest corresponds to length minus k.
column4: Advance past a value swapped in from the larger partition without examining it.~That new value is still unclassified.

column2: Return the cooldown block formula even when it is smaller than the task count.~At least one interval is required for every task.
column3: Ignore how many task types share the maximum frequency.~All equally frequent types contribute to the final partial block.
column4: Multiply the number of tasks by n plus one.~Different task types can fill cooldown gaps, so that overcounts idle time.

column2: Include only followed users' tweets and omit the user's own tweets.~A user's own tweets belong in the news feed too.
column3: Rank candidates by tweet ID instead of posting time.~Tweet identifiers do not define recency.
column4: Take one tweet from each user and stop.~Several of the ten newest tweets may come from one user's stream.

column2: Pick the shortest task even if it has not arrived yet.~Only tasks available at the current time can be selected.
column3: Break equal processing-time ties by arrival time.~Ties use the original task index.
column4: Advance the clock only by completed work and wait forever on an empty queue.~When no task is available, time jumps to the next arrival.

column2: Immediately return the chosen character to the candidate pool before the next choice.~It could be chosen twice consecutively.
column3: Group all copies of each letter together.~Repeated adjacent characters violate the output condition.
column4: Always alternate the two most common letters and discard the rest.~Every input character occurrence must be used in a valid rearrangement.

column2: Always choose the most frequent letter even after using it twice in a row.~A third equal consecutive letter is forbidden.
column3: Stop as soon as the largest-count letter is temporarily blocked.~Another available letter may allow a longer valid result.
column4: Require all letters to be exhausted even if none can be appended legally.~Some inputs cannot use every occurrence without creating a triple.

column2: Add passengers at both pickup and drop-off positions.~Drop-offs reduce occupancy.
column3: Reject whenever the total passengers across all trips exceeds capacity.~Non-overlapping trips can reuse the same seats.
column4: Check occupancy only after the final trip's endpoint.~Capacity can be exceeded at an earlier location and later fall again.

column2: Split arriving numbers by their arrival index only.~The two heaps must represent lower and upper values, not alternating arrivals.
column3: Balance sizes but ignore whether lower-half values exceed upper-half values.~Correct median boundaries require both ordering and size invariants.
column4: Always average both heap roots even for odd total size.~With odd size the extra element's heap root is the median.

column2: Choose the largest profit from all projects immediately.~The required capital must be affordable before the project can start.
column3: Spend all available capital when choosing a project.~Required capital is an eligibility threshold; the project adds its profit to capital.
column4: Choose exactly k projects even when none is affordable.~The task permits at most k projects and must stop if no feasible candidate exists.

column2: XOR all numbers once and return that value.~The task sums XOR results over every subset, including smaller selections.
column3: Add each value to the running subset total instead of applying XOR.~Subset scores use bitwise XOR, not arithmetic addition.
column4: Explore only subsets containing the first element.~Every include-or-exclude decision contributes valid subsets.

column2: Record only selections using every input value.~Subsets of all sizes, including empty, belong in the output.
column3: Restart choices from index zero at every depth.~That can reuse positions and generate order duplicates.
column4: Store the same mutable selection object for every answer.~Later undo operations would change previously recorded subsets.

column2: Advance past a chosen candidate so it can never be reused.~This version allows repeated use of a candidate.
column3: Restart from the first candidate after every choice.~That generates permutations of the same combination as duplicate answers.
column4: Record a choice as soon as its sum exceeds the target.~With positive candidates, an overshoot cannot become a valid combination.

column2: Allow a chosen candidate index to be reused recursively.~Each input occurrence may be used at most once.
column3: Remove all duplicate values before searching.~Distinct occurrences of the same value may both be needed in one combination.
column4: Ignore equal choices at the same recursion depth.~That repeats the same value combination through interchangeable indices.

column2: Generate all orderings of k different numbers.~Combinations do not distinguish the order of the same selected values.
column3: Allow the same number to be chosen repeatedly.~A combination selects distinct numbers from 1 through n.
column4: Record every partial selection before it reaches k numbers.~Every returned combination must have exactly k elements.

column2: Only choose later indices after the previous choice.~That generates combinations instead of every ordering.
column3: Allow an input index to be chosen more than once in a permutation.~Every original position must appear exactly once.
column4: Keep used indices marked after returning from a branch.~Sibling branches need those positions available again.

column2: Remove duplicate input values before generating subsets.~A subset may legitimately contain several occurrences of one value.
column3: Never skip equal sibling choices.~Equivalent choices at the same depth repeat identical subsets.
column4: Skip equal values at every depth, even after selecting their predecessor.~That wrongly prevents subsets containing multiple duplicate occurrences.

column2: Use each distinct value only once in each permutation.~Duplicate occurrences still have to appear in every complete permutation.
column3: Generate every index permutation without skipping interchangeable equal choices.~Several index permutations produce the same value ordering.
column4: Keep the used marks from a completed permutation.~That blocks the positions needed to construct later permutations.

column2: Generate strings with n openers and n closers without checking prefixes.~A prefix with more closers than openers can never form valid parentheses.
column3: Append all openers followed by all closers and return only that string.~Other valid arrangements must also be generated.
column4: Allow a closing bracket whenever fewer than n closers were used.~There must also be an unmatched opener available to close.

column2: Keep one global visited set across all starting paths.~A cell rejected in one path may be needed in another independent path.
column3: Permit revisiting a cell later in the same word path.~A board cell can be used only once per candidate word.
column4: Move diagonally as well as horizontally and vertically.~The word path permits only the four orthogonal neighbors.

column2: Choose only the longest palindromic prefix at every position.~All valid partitions are required, including those beginning with shorter pieces.
column3: Require the entire original string to be a palindrome.~A non-palindromic string can still be partitioned into palindromic pieces.
column4: Record a partition before its pieces consume the whole string.~The pieces must cover the input completely without gaps.

column2: Choose one letter total from any digit's mapping.~A combination needs one letter from every digit, in order.
column3: Sort the digits before generating letters.~Digit positions determine the character positions in each result.
column4: Always pick the first mapped letter and never branch.~That misses other valid combinations.

column2: Accept whenever the total length is divisible by four.~The individual sticks may still be impossible to partition into four equal sides.
column3: Cut an oversized stick to fill the remaining side space.~Sticks cannot be broken.
column4: Put each stick on the currently shortest side and never reconsider.~A locally fitting placement may block a later valid partition.

column2: Accept whenever the total is divisible by k.~Divisibility is necessary but does not guarantee a feasible partition.
column3: Split the sorted array into k equal-length groups.~Subsets must have equal sums, not necessarily equal counts.
column4: Assign each number to its first fitting bucket without backtracking.~A different earlier placement may be needed to complete all buckets.

column2: Place one queen per row while checking only columns.~Diagonal attacks must also be excluded.
column3: Keep occupied-column marks after undoing a queen.~That wrongly prevents columns from being reused in sibling search branches.
column4: Record only the first complete board.~The task requests all distinct valid boards.

column2: Return the number of safe positions in the first row.~Each first-row choice can lead to multiple or no complete boards.
column3: Count a placement as soon as the current row has a safe column.~Only complete placements of n queens contribute to the answer.
column4: Check only one diagonal direction.~Queens attack along both row-minus-column and row-plus-column diagonals.

column2: Return only whether a segmentation exists.~This problem requests every valid sentence, not a boolean.
column3: Memoize results by word length alone.~Different start positions can have different suffixes even with equal-length chosen words.
column4: Choose only the longest dictionary prefix and discard shorter alternatives.~Several prefix choices may lead to different valid sentences.

column2: Treat every traversed prefix as a complete stored word.~Search needs an end-of-word marker distinct from prefix existence.
column3: Store one whole word per first-character branch.~Words can share longer prefixes and diverge later.
column4: Restart traversal from the root for every character.~Each character must advance from the previous prefix node.

column2: Treat a dot as a literal stored character.~A dot matches any one letter and must explore character children.
column3: Return true after matching a prefix even without an end marker.~The query must match a whole stored word.
column4: Let a dot consume any number of characters.~Each dot matches exactly one character.

column2: Choose the longest dictionary match greedily and skip all other matches.~A shorter match can allow better coverage of the remaining string.
column3: Count a character as extra only if it occurs in no dictionary word.~A letter's presence somewhere does not mean it can be covered at its current position.
column4: Reject the whole string when no word covers its first character.~Extra characters are allowed and should be counted, not treated as failure.

column2: Return a word every time any path reaches its end marker.~The result must contain each found word only once.
column3: Mark board cells permanently after exploring one word prefix.~Other starting paths need those cells restored.
column4: Discard a trie branch immediately after finding one word on it.~Longer words can share that prefix, so remaining descendants may still be needed.

column2: Count only land cells on the outside border of the grid.~Water boundaries inside the grid also contribute to perimeter.
column3: Subtract one for each shared side counted from above or left.~Adding four per cell counts a shared side twice, so it removes two perimeter sides.
column4: Use the number of land cells as the perimeter.~Different land arrangements with equal area can have different boundary lengths.

column2: Compare words using the language's default alphabet order.~The supplied alien ranking defines the order.
column3: Compare every unequal position even after the first mismatch decides the order.~Lexicographic order is decided by the first differing character.
column4: Accept a longer word before its exact shorter prefix.~The shorter prefix must appear first.

column2: Choose the person with the most incoming trust, even if it is fewer than n-1.~The judge must be trusted by every other person.
column3: Ignore outgoing trust when choosing the judge.~The judge must trust nobody.
column4: Return the person with outgoing trust to everyone else.~That is the reverse of the judge's required role.

column2: Count every land cell as a separate island.~Orthogonally connected land belongs to one island.
column3: Connect diagonal land cells too.~Islands use horizontal and vertical adjacency only.
column4: Mark a cell after recursively exploring all its neighbors.~Neighbor recursion can revisit the current cell before it is marked.

column2: Count the number of islands instead of their sizes.~The answer is the largest component's cell count.
column3: Add the areas of all disconnected islands.~Only one connected island contributes to the maximum area.
column4: Allow a visited cell to contribute again from another neighbor.~That double-counts area and may recurse indefinitely.

column2: Copy nodes but attach their original neighbors.~A deep clone must contain cloned neighbor identities.
column3: Create the clone map entry only after all neighbor recursion finishes.~A graph cycle can return to the original before its clone has been recorded.
column4: Identify nodes only by their traversal position.~The same original node reached by different paths must reuse one clone.

column2: Start from one gate and ignore the others.~A room may be closer to a different gate.
column3: Increase distance once for every processed room.~Distance advances by path steps, not total queue removals.
column4: Allow traversal through walls.~Walls block movement and must never receive room distances.

column2: Start rotting from only the first rotten orange.~All initially rotten oranges spread simultaneously.
column3: Count one minute for every orange that becomes rotten.~Many oranges can rot during the same distance layer.
column4: Return elapsed time even if fresh oranges remain unreachable.~An unreachable fresh orange requires a result of minus one.

column2: Explore downhill from the ocean borders.~Reverse reachability must go to equal or higher cells that can flow back down.
column3: Return cells reached from either ocean.~A qualifying cell must reach both oceans.
column4: Combine both oceans into one visited set without tracking their origins.~Then it is impossible to distinguish one-ocean reachability from both-ocean reachability.

column2: Flip every O that is not directly on the border.~Interior cells connected to border O cells are safe too.
column3: Mark safe cells only along the outermost row.~All four borders can protect connected regions.
column4: Restore all original O cells after the traversal.~Only the marked border-connected cells should be restored; enclosed regions must flip.

column2: Move every wheel one step together in a single move.~A move changes exactly one wheel.
column3: Ignore visited states and repeatedly enqueue every legal neighbor.~Cycles can cause unbounded repeated exploration.
column4: Return the first depth-first path length found.~The first depth-first path need not use the fewest moves.

column2: Start with arbitrary courses even if they still have prerequisites.~Only zero-indegree courses are currently available.
column3: Accept whenever at least one course can be removed.~A separate cycle may prevent completing the remaining courses.
column4: Increase dependents' indegrees when a prerequisite is completed.~Completing a prerequisite removes one unmet requirement.

column2: Return courses in their numeric order.~Numeric labels do not express prerequisite order.
column3: Return the partial removal order even when a cycle remains.~The output must contain every course or report impossibility.
column4: Build edges from course to prerequisite and use the same removal order.~That reverses the dependency ordering of the selected construction.

column2: Reject every visited neighbor, including the node's parent.~An undirected edge back to the parent is expected and is not a cycle.
column3: Accept when the component containing zero has no cycle.~The graph must also be connected across all n vertices.
column4: Check only that the graph has n-1 edges.~That count alone does not rule out a cycle plus a disconnected component.

column2: Treat a prerequisite relation as bidirectional.~Prerequisite reachability follows directed edges only.
column3: Answer true only for directly listed prerequisite pairs.~Indirect chains also establish prerequisites.
column4: Use one shared reachability row for all starting courses.~Each start has its own set of reachable courses.

column2: Start only one traversal from vertex zero and return one.~Other disconnected components may exist.
column3: Count only vertices that appear in an edge.~Isolated vertices are components too.
column4: Treat undirected edges as one-way links.~Component connectivity must be traversable in either direction.

column2: Return the first edge that lies on any cycle in forward order.~When multiple cycle edges qualify, the last input edge is required.
column3: Keep the candidate edge available during its connectivity test.~Its endpoints would always appear connected by that very edge.
column4: Return an edge whose endpoints become disconnected when it is skipped.~Such an edge is necessary for connectivity and is not redundant.

column2: Merge all accounts with the same name.~Different people can have the same name; shared emails establish identity.
column3: Merge only directly overlapping pairs without following chains.~Accounts connected transitively through other accounts also form one group.
column4: Keep repeated email occurrences in the merged output.~Each email should appear once per merged component.

column2: Add ratios along a query path.~Equation ratios compose by multiplication.
column3: Add the same weight to both directions of an equation edge.~The reverse direction uses the reciprocal ratio.
column4: Return one for an unknown variable divided by itself.~A variable absent from the graph is still unknown and returns minus one.

column2: Choose every original leaf as a minimum-height root.~The best roots are central, reached after trimming leaf layers.
column3: Remove newly exposed leaves immediately in the same layer.~Simultaneous layers are needed to preserve the tree's centers.
column4: Trim until no vertices remain.~A tree's center consists of one or two vertices and should be retained.

column2: Allow a move that changes several letters at once.~Each valid transformation changes exactly one character.
column3: Use a depth-first search and return its first successful chain length.~The first depth-first chain may not be shortest.
column4: Count only transformations and omit the starting word from the reported length.~The requested sequence length includes both endpoint words.

column2: Add all height differences along the path.~Effort is the largest single edge difference, not their sum.
column3: Minimize the number of steps regardless of heights.~A longer path can have a much smaller maximum height change.
column4: Mark a cell optimal merely when it is first seen without comparing effort.~For this edge-weight problem, a later path can improve a tentative effort.

column2: Return the smallest arrival time among reached nodes.~The signal must reach everyone, so the latest shortest arrival determines delay.
column3: Use an unweighted BFS level as the travel time.~Edge weights are not necessarily equal.
column4: Return the largest reached time even when some nodes are unreachable.~If any node is unreachable, the required result is minus one.

column2: Append each next airport immediately and never revise dead ends.~A lexical choice can end early; finishing-order assembly preserves all tickets.
column3: Mark airports visited and forbid revisiting them.~Airports may repeat; tickets, not vertices, are consumed once.
column4: Deduplicate identical tickets before constructing the graph.~Repeated tickets are distinct edges that must each be used.

column2: Connect each point only to its nearest neighbor and stop.~Those choices can leave multiple disconnected components.
column3: Accept the cheapest n-1 edges without checking cycles.~A cycle can waste an edge while another point remains disconnected.
column4: Minimize squared Euclidean distance instead of Manhattan distance.~The edge cost is the sum of absolute coordinate differences.

column2: Sum every elevation along the path.~The required time is the highest elevation encountered.
column3: Use the shortest number of grid moves as the answer.~A short route may require a higher water level than a longer route.
column4: Ignore the starting cell's elevation.~The water must already cover the starting cell too.

column2: Add an ordering edge for every differing character position in adjacent words.~Only the first differing position determines lexical precedence.
column3: Ignore characters that never appear in a differing pair.~They still belong in the returned alphabet order.
column4: Accept a longer word before its exact prefix.~No alphabet ordering can make that input ordering valid.

column2: Relax prices in place within each round.~One round could then chain many flights and exceed the edge budget.
column3: Run only k relaxation rounds.~K intermediate stops permit up to k+1 flights.
column4: Choose the unconstrained cheapest route and ignore stops.~That route may use more stops than allowed.

column2: Call every edge in one computed MST critical.~An alternative MST may replace some of those edges at the same cost.
column3: Call an edge pseudo-critical merely because excluding it preserves the cost.~It must also be possible to force that edge into some minimum-cost tree.
column4: Compare excluded-edge costs without checking whether the graph remains connected.~Disconnection means no spanning tree and is evidence of criticality.

column2: Use one topological order for both rows and columns.~The two independent sets of conditions can require different orders.
column3: Place every number on the diagonal regardless of the conditions.~Row and column positions must satisfy their respective precedence constraints.
column4: Return a partial matrix when only some numbers appear in an order.~A cycle makes the full arrangement impossible.

column2: Require every pair of values to have GCD greater than one directly.~Indirect paths through other indices are allowed.
column3: Accept whenever all values are greater than one.~Different prime-factor components can still be disconnected.
column4: Treat repeated values as one index and ignore isolated occurrences of one.~Every original index must be reachable; one has no shared prime factor.

column2: Return n because each stair provides one choice.~One- and two-step moves form different sequences; their counts follow a recurrence.
column3: Track only the previous count and double it every time.~The last move can come from two different prior stair states, not two copies of one state.
column4: Replace both previous counts before saving the old one.~The next recurrence needs the two distinct earlier values.

column2: Always step onto the cheaper of the next two raw-cost stairs.~A cheap immediate stair can lead to expensive future costs.
column3: Require starting on stair zero.~The problem permits starting at stair zero or stair one.
column4: Return only the final stair's cost.~The result includes every paid stair along the selected route.

column2: Sum only the previous two values.~Tribonacci depends on the previous three values.
column3: Use one for the zeroth value.~The specified initial value T0 is zero.
column4: Update the three variables one by one using newly overwritten values.~Each next value must use all three values from the previous state.

column2: Take every house with positive value.~Adjacent houses cannot both be robbed.
column3: Take either all even-index houses or all odd-index houses, whichever totals more.~A valid optimal selection can switch parity after skipping additional houses.
column4: Compare robbing a house with only the previous house's value.~The comparison must use the best totals for whole prefixes.

column2: Run the linear recurrence on the full circle without exclusions.~It can choose both first and last houses, which are adjacent.
column3: Exclude both the first and last houses at once.~An optimal solution may include either one; only their joint inclusion is forbidden.
column4: Add the answers from the two excluded-end cases.~Those are alternative plans, not disjoint gains that can be combined.

column2: Expand only from single-character centers.~Even-length palindromes require centers between adjacent characters.
column3: Count all palindromes and return that count.~This problem asks for a longest palindromic substring itself.
column4: Allow unmatched interior characters as long as the endpoints agree.~Every mirrored pair inside the substring must match.

column2: Count only the longest palindrome around each center.~Every successful shorter expansion is a distinct substring occurrence too.
column3: Store palindrome texts in a set and return the set size.~Equal text at different positions counts as different substrings.
column4: Expand only from adjacent-pair centers.~Odd-length palindromes, including single characters, also count.

column2: Treat every single digit, including zero, as one letter.~Zero has no standalone letter decoding.
column3: Allow any two-digit number below 100.~Valid two-digit codes are only 10 through 26.
column4: Use zero ways for the empty suffix.~A fully consumed string contributes one completed decoding.

column2: Always take the largest coin that fits.~For arbitrary denominations, that greedy choice can miss a smaller coin count or a solution.
column3: Store zero for every initially unreachable positive amount.~Zero would falsely claim those amounts need no coins.
column4: Count every way to make the amount instead of minimizing coin count.~The objective is the fewest coins, not the number of combinations.

column2: Track only the largest product ending at each position.~A very negative product can become the largest after multiplication by another negative value.
column3: Discard every negative product permanently.~Two negatives can produce a strong positive candidate later.
column4: Return zero whenever the input includes zero.~A different segment may have a positive product larger than zero.

column2: Choose the longest matching dictionary word at each position and never backtrack.~A shorter prefix may permit a valid segmentation when the longer one does not.
column3: Accept when every character appears somewhere in the dictionary.~Word boundaries and exact contiguous matches are required.
column4: Initialize the empty prefix as impossible.~The first matched dictionary word needs a valid empty prefix to extend.

column2: Sort the input and return its number of distinct values.~Sorting destroys the subsequence's required original order.
column3: Append equal values to the tails list as new lengths.~The subsequence must be strictly increasing.
column4: Return the final tails list as the requested sequence.~This task asks for the length; the tails summary need not itself be one original subsequence.

column2: Put each value into the currently lighter group and never revise.~Greedy balancing can miss a valid partition.
column3: Update the same reachable-sum set while using its newly added sums again for this value.~That can reuse the current number more than once.
column4: Return true whenever the total sum is even.~An even total may have no subset equal to half of it.

column2: Process each number outside the amount loop to count unordered combinations.~This task distinguishes different orders of the same chosen numbers.
column3: Set the number of ways to make zero to zero.~The empty sequence is the base way that extends into nonempty sequences.
column4: Use each input number at most once.~Numbers may be reused in a sequence.

column2: Always subtract the largest square that fits.~A greedy choice need not minimize the number of squares.
column3: Allow only distinct square values.~The same square can be used repeatedly.
column4: Minimize the sum of the chosen squares rather than their count.~Every valid solution must sum to n; the optimization is over the number of terms.

column2: Keep n unsplit whenever it has the largest value.~At least two positive integers must be used.
column3: Keep extracting threes even when that leaves a final one.~Replacing 3+1 by 2+2 gives a larger product.
column4: Split into only ones to maximize the number of pieces.~Many pieces do not imply a large product; multiplying by one adds no gain.

column2: Always take the three available stones with the largest immediate total.~The opponent's future advantage and negative values can change the best choice.
column3: Add the opponent's best remaining advantage to the current gain.~The opponent's score reduces the current player's advantage and must be subtracted.
column4: Sort the stone values before choosing groups.~Players must take the next stones from the front in their original order.

column2: Multiply the number of rows by the number of columns.~That counts cells, not distinct paths.
column3: Add diagonal predecessors as another path source.~Only right and down moves are permitted.
column4: Overwrite a cell's count with the left count only.~Paths arriving from above must be included too.

column2: Leave a blocked cell's previous path count unchanged.~No path may pass through an obstacle, so its count becomes zero.
column3: Treat obstacles as an extra movement cost instead of a barrier.~These cells are impassable, not merely expensive.
column4: Initialize every cell in the first row to one even beyond an obstacle.~An obstacle blocks all further paths along that initial row unless another route exists.

column2: Choose the cheaper immediate neighbor at each move.~A locally cheap cell can lead to a more expensive remaining path.
column3: Add both predecessor path sums together.~Only one predecessor belongs to a single minimum-cost path.
column4: Permit moves back upward to reduce the cost.~The problem permits only right and down moves.

column2: Require matching characters to occupy adjacent positions in both strings.~A subsequence can skip characters.
column3: On a mismatch, discard one character from both strings together.~The best answer may require skipping from only one side.
column4: Count all matching character pairs without preserving order.~Subsequence positions must increase in both strings.

column2: Always smash the two largest remaining stones.~That is the fixed process in a different problem; here choosing pairs can produce a better residual.
column3: Assume an even total always permits a residual of zero.~The available stone weights may not form equal-sum subsets.
column4: Use a stone repeatedly while constructing a subset sum.~Each stone belongs to one group exactly once.

column2: Buy immediately on the day after every sale when the price is attractive.~That violates the mandatory cooldown day.
column3: Compute holding profit from the just-updated resting state.~It can accidentally reuse same-day transitions and bypass the cooldown.
column4: Return the holding state's profit as a final realized gain.~An unsold stock has not realized its sale value; the final answer is a non-holding state.

column2: Loop over amounts first and count each possible final coin.~That counts ordered sequences, overcounting combinations with the same coins.
column3: Walk amounts downward for each coin.~That permits each coin only once instead of unlimited reuse.
column4: Set zero ways to make amount zero.~The empty combination is the one base way from which others are built.

column2: Track reachable sums in a set and discard their multiplicities.~Different sign assignments can reach the same sum and must all be counted.
column3: Assign only plus signs to nonnegative values.~Every occurrence needs both plus and minus choices.
column4: Merge new sums into the old map while still processing the same number.~That may apply one occurrence repeatedly within the same step.

column2: Compare only the combined character counts of the three strings.~Each source string's internal order must also be preserved.
column3: Whenever both sources match, always consume from the first.~The second choice may be necessary for a successful later continuation.
column4: Require the combined string to be the first source followed by the second.~Valid interleavings can switch between sources many times.

column2: Always take the larger visible end pile.~That can expose a better remaining game for the opponent.
column3: Add the opponent's remaining advantage to the current pile.~An opponent's advantage counts against the current player.
column4: Sort the piles and assign alternating values.~Players can take only the current ends in the original arrangement.

column2: Always take the maximum 2M piles immediately.~Leaving a different suffix can produce a better final score.
column3: Memoize only by pile index and ignore M.~The legal future move range also depends on M.
column4: Keep M fixed at its initial value.~After taking x piles, the next state's M is max(M,x).

column2: Allow movement to equal-valued neighbors.~The path must be strictly increasing; equality can also introduce cycles.
column3: Cache one answer for each matrix value, regardless of its position.~Equal values at different cells can have different reachable neighbors.
column4: Choose the largest immediate neighbor and ignore the others.~A smaller increasing neighbor may lead to a longer path.

column2: Count each matched target text only once.~Different source index selections are distinct subsequences even when the text is identical.
column3: When characters match, discard the option of skipping the source character.~Both using and skipping a matching occurrence may lead to valid distinct subsequences.
column4: Set zero ways to form the empty target.~Every source prefix has one way to form the empty target: choose nothing.

column2: Count only differing characters at matching positions.~Insertions and deletions can shift alignment and improve the edit count.
column3: Allow replacement but ignore insertion and deletion.~All three edit operations belong in the recurrence.
column4: Initialize all empty-prefix distances to zero.~Converting an empty prefix to a nonempty one costs its length.

column2: Always burst the currently largest balloon first.~Its value interacts with changing neighbors, so local value alone is not sufficient.
column3: Choose the first balloon in an interval while assuming its original neighbors stay fixed.~Bursting first changes adjacency; the last-burst formulation keeps interval boundaries fixed.
column4: Ignore the artificial outer balloons of value one.~Those boundaries are needed for gains involving the original first and last balloons.

column2: Treat star as an independent wildcard matching any text.~Star repeats its preceding token, rather than matching arbitrary characters itself.
column3: Require every star to match at least one character.~Zero repetitions are allowed.
column4: Accept when the pattern matches only a prefix of the string.~The entire string must match the entire pattern.

column2: Use a twenty-dollar bill to make change for a later customer.~All required change is fifteen dollars or less, so twenties cannot help form it.
column3: For a twenty, always spend three fives even when ten plus five is available.~Preserving fives can be essential for later ten-dollar payments.
column4: Count all bills in advance before serving the first customer.~Change can use only money already received.

column2: Return the sum of all positive values wherever they occur.~The chosen subarray must be contiguous.
column3: Initialize the best answer to zero and allow choosing no values.~The required subarray is nonempty, including in all-negative input.
column4: Discard a running prefix whenever the next value is negative.~A negative value can connect two positive segments into the best contiguous sum.

column2: Always return total minus the minimum subarray sum.~The best answer may not wrap, and all-negative input needs special handling.
column3: Concatenate the array twice and allow a subarray of any length.~A valid circular subarray may not reuse an element.
column4: Use zero as a valid empty wrapped answer for all-negative input.~A nonempty subarray is required.

column2: Keep extending whenever adjacent values are unequal.~The comparison direction must alternate, not merely stay nonzero.
column3: Continue the previous turbulent length through equal adjacent values.~Equality breaks both possible alternating directions.
column4: Track only increasing endings.~A decreasing comparison needs the previous increasing state, and vice versa.

column2: Jump to the farthest immediate landing position at every step.~A shorter landing can have a much greater future reach.
column3: Extend reach using every array value even if its index is unreachable.~An inaccessible position cannot help extend the reachable frontier.
column4: Return false whenever any value is zero.~A zero can be jumped over or can be the final destination.
