column2: Count one jump for every index scanned.~Several positions belong to the same jump-distance layer.
column3: Choose the largest jump value without considering its index.~Reach is index plus jump length, and choices must be reachable.
column4: Increment the jump count again upon scanning the destination.~Reaching the last index does not require another jump away from it.

column2: Treat every zero character as reachable.~A valid chain of jump distances must lead to that position.
column3: Keep all previously reachable positions in the candidate count forever.~Positions more than maxJump away must expire.
column4: Consider only jumps of exactly maxJump.~Any distance from minJump through maxJump may be necessary.

column2: Choose the station with the largest gas value.~Its outgoing cost and the rest of the route also matter.
column3: Restart at the same station where the tank first becomes negative.~That station is within the failed segment; the new candidate starts after it.
column4: Return a local starting candidate without checking total gas against total cost.~No starting point can complete the circuit when total fuel is insufficient.

column2: Check only that the hand size is divisible by groupSize.~The individual card counts must support consecutive groups too.
column3: Build groups from arbitrary large cards before handling the smallest remaining card.~The smallest remaining card has no lower unused predecessor and must start a group.
column4: Reuse one card occurrence in several groups.~Each occurrence must be consumed exactly once.

column2: Declare the party with more initial senators the winner.~Turn order and bans can let a smaller party win.
column3: Requeue a surviving senator at the same turn index.~Its next action belongs in the next round, after remaining current turns.
column4: Let both senators act before applying either ban.~The earlier senator removes the later one's opportunity to act.

column2: Take each coordinate from any triplet, including ones exceeding other target coordinates.~Coordinatewise maximum cannot undo an excessive coordinate.
column3: Require one input triplet to equal the target completely.~Different usable triplets can supply different target coordinates.
column4: Accept as soon as any one target coordinate is matched.~All three target coordinates must be attainable.

column2: Close a partition when the current character reaches its own last occurrence.~Another character already in the partition may occur later.
column3: Split into fixed-length parts.~Part boundaries depend on the characters' final occurrences.
column4: Return the number of partitions rather than their lengths.~The required result lists each partition's size.

column2: Treat every star as an opening parenthesis.~A valid assignment may require a closing parenthesis or an empty choice.
column3: Track only the total counts at the end.~A prefix may contain too many closers even if totals could balance later.
column4: Reject whenever the minimum possible open count would go negative.~The minimum can be clamped to zero because stars may be empty or opening.

column2: Use only a left-to-right increasing-rating pass.~A decreasing sequence also needs constraints from the right neighbor.
column3: During the right-to-left pass, overwrite previously larger candy counts with smaller ones.~That can undo the left-neighbor constraint already satisfied.
column4: Give equal ratings different candy counts in sorted rating order only.~Constraints apply to original neighbors, and equal ratings impose no strict inequality.

column2: Append the new interval at the end without merging.~Its correct position and any overlaps must be resolved.
column3: Merge only the first overlapping interval.~The new interval may overlap a whole chain of existing intervals.
column4: Treat touching closed intervals as disjoint.~For this problem, touching endpoints belong to one merged interval.

column2: Merge intervals only when their starts are equal.~Intervals with different starts can still overlap.
column3: Process unsorted intervals while comparing only with the previous output interval.~An overlap with an earlier interval can be missed without ordering.
column4: Replace an overlapping interval's end with the next end unconditionally.~A contained interval has a smaller end and must not shrink the union.

column2: On an overlap, keep the interval with the larger end.~The earlier-ending interval leaves more room for future intervals.
column3: Remove both overlapping intervals every time.~Removing just one may be sufficient and gives a smaller removal count.
column4: Treat meetings that touch at endpoints as overlapping.~An interval ending when another begins does not overlap in this problem.

column2: Check only whether two meetings have identical start times.~Meetings with different starts can still overlap.
column3: Treat a start equal to the previous end as a conflict.~Back-to-back meetings are allowed.
column4: Sort by duration and check neighboring entries.~Chronological start order is needed for the adjacent-overlap check.

column2: Count overlapping pairs and add one.~Pair counts do not equal the maximum number of simultaneous meetings.
column3: Reuse a room only when its end is strictly before the next start.~A room is available when its meeting ends exactly at the next start too.
column4: Track only the last processed meeting's end.~Any previously allocated room may become available, so the earliest end must be accessible.

column2: When all rooms are busy, cancel the waiting meeting.~It must be delayed until a room becomes available.
column3: Delay the start but keep the original end unchanged.~The full original duration must be preserved.
column4: Break room-availability ties using the largest room number.~The rules choose the lowest-numbered room.

column2: Return the first interval that contains each query.~The answer needs the shortest containing interval.
column3: Keep expired intervals eligible in the heap.~An interval ending before the query does not contain it.
column4: Return answers in sorted-query order.~Results must be mapped back to each query's original position.

column2: Use an ordinary zero-based base-26 digit rule without subtracting one.~Column letters are one-based: 26 is Z, not BA.
column3: Emit least-significant letters without reversing them.~Digits are extracted backward but must be returned most significant first.
column4: Use decimal digits for remainders ten through twenty-five.~Every remainder maps to a letter A through Z.

column2: Return a prefix of GCD length without checking repetition compatibility.~Equal length factors alone do not guarantee both strings repeat that prefix.
column3: Use the longest common prefix as the divisor automatically.~That prefix may not tile both strings completely.
column4: Choose the smaller input length whenever any common character exists.~A divisor must reproduce each entire string by repetition.

column2: After insertion, advance to the newly inserted GCD node.~The task inserts once between original adjacent pairs, not repeatedly between new pairs.
column3: Replace each original node value with a GCD.~Original nodes and their values must remain in the list.
column4: Insert only between the first two nodes.~Every original adjacent pair needs its own inserted node.

column2: Allocate the output with the same dimensions for every matrix.~A non-square transpose swaps its row and column counts.
column3: Reverse each row without swapping coordinates.~That is a horizontal reflection, not a transpose.
column4: Swap every pair twice in a full two-dimensional loop.~Double swapping restores the original values and also fails for rectangular shapes.

column2: Transpose the matrix and stop.~That reflects across the diagonal; reversing rows completes the clockwise rotation.
column3: Transpose by swapping every pair in both directions.~Each off-diagonal pair would be swapped twice and end unchanged.
column4: Reverse rows before transposing while keeping the same claimed clockwise direction.~That order produces the opposite rotation.

column2: Traverse every row left to right.~Spiral order follows shrinking outer boundaries instead.
column3: Read all four sides without checking whether a row or column has collapsed.~Single-row or single-column remainders can then be duplicated.
column4: Leave the boundaries unchanged after visiting a side.~Previously visited cells would be processed again.

column2: Zero a full row and column immediately whenever a zero is encountered.~Newly created zeros can trigger unintended cascades.
column3: Use the first row and column as markers without remembering their original zeros.~Their own final treatment cannot then be distinguished from marker writes.
column4: Clear only the cells that were originally zero.~Every row and column containing an original zero must be cleared.

column2: Stop only when the state reaches one, without detecting cycles.~Unhappy numbers enter a non-one cycle and would never terminate.
column3: Sum the digits rather than their squares.~The required transformation sums squared digits.
column4: Declare every meeting between fast and slow states happy.~A meeting may identify an unhappy cycle; happiness requires reaching one.

column2: Increase the final digit without propagating a carry.~A final nine becomes zero and must carry left.
column3: Discard overflow beyond the first digit.~An all-nine input needs a new leading one.
column4: Increase every digit by one.~Only the original added one and its resulting carry propagate.

column2: Always add every Roman symbol's value.~Subtractive pairs such as IV require subtracting the smaller preceding value.
column3: Subtract a symbol whenever it is smaller than any later symbol.~The rule compares with the immediately following symbol, not an arbitrary later one.
column4: Subtract a symbol when the previous symbol is smaller than it.~The smaller preceding symbol is the one to subtract, not the larger symbol that follows it.

column2: Multiply the base by the exponent.~Exponentiation is repeated multiplication, not scalar multiplication.
column3: Ignore negative exponents.~A negative exponent requires the reciprocal of the positive power.
column4: Square the accumulated result every round regardless of the exponent bits.~The algorithm squares the base and includes it in the result only for selected bits.

column2: Convert both entire strings to fixed-precision numbers before multiplying.~Large inputs can exceed numeric precision; the chosen method operates on individual digits.
column3: Place every digit-pair product into one shared output position.~Each pair contributes according to the sum of its place indices.
column4: Store raw products as digits without carrying.~Each output position must hold a decimal digit with excess carried left.

column2: Count each distinct corner only once, ignoring duplicate points.~Stored multiplicities create additional valid square combinations.
column3: Allow a horizontal partner at the same x-coordinate as the query.~That gives a zero-length side, which is not a square.
column4: Check only squares above the query's row.~Valid squares can also extend below it.

column2: Add all values instead of XORing them.~Arithmetic addition does not cancel equal pairs.
column3: Use bitwise OR to combine values.~OR preserves shared set bits instead of canceling paired values.
column4: Return the smallest input value.~The unpaired value is unrelated to numeric ordering.

column2: Count iterations while repeatedly dividing n by two.~That counts bit positions, including zero bits, rather than only ones.
column3: Clear the highest bit without counting the others.~Every set bit must contribute to the result.
column4: Use n AND n-plus-one as the clear operation.~That does not consistently clear exactly the lowest set bit.

column2: Set every positive number's count to one.~Many numbers contain multiple set bits.
column3: Reuse the count of i-minus-one and always add one.~Crossing a power-of-two boundary can clear several lower bits.
column4: Return only the bit count for n.~The task requests counts for every value from zero through n.

column2: Add corresponding digits from the left without aligning their ends.~Binary place values align at the rightmost digits.
column3: Ignore the carry after both strings are consumed.~The final carry can create a new leading bit.
column4: Use decimal carry rules with remainder ten.~Binary digits and carries use base two.

column2: Stop as soon as the remaining input becomes zero.~Leading zero positions still matter in a fixed 32-bit reversal.
column3: Reverse only the decimal digits of n.~The requested representation is binary with exactly 32 positions.
column4: Shift the result right before appending each input bit.~The result must make space on its right by shifting left.

column2: XOR only the input values without the expected full range.~The missing value is isolated by canceling against all expected values.
column3: Use expected values from zero through n minus one only.~The expected range includes n even though the final input index is n minus one.
column4: Return the last array index absent as a value without considering n.~The missing number may be n, which is beyond the last array index.

column2: Use XOR once and ignore carries.~XOR computes only the sum without carried bits.
column3: Use OR to compute the carry positions.~Carries arise where both inputs have a one, which requires AND.
column4: Shift the carry bits right instead of left.~A carry contributes to the next higher bit position.

column2: Reverse the decimal digits and return any resulting integer.~Overflow beyond the signed 32-bit range must return zero.
column3: Drop the sign before reversing and always return a positive result.~Negative inputs require a negative reversed result.
column4: Check overflow only before extracting the first digit.~Every appended digit can newly cross a signed bound.

column2: Compute only left AND right.~An interior number can clear a bit that is set in both endpoints.
column3: Use bitwise OR across the range.~The operation required is AND, preserving only bits common to every value.
column4: Return the shared prefix without shifting it back.~Its original high-bit positions must be restored.

column2: Add n minus one directly to x.~Ordinary addition can clear bits of x that must remain set in every value.
column3: Write sequence bits into every bit position, including x's ones.~Only zero-bit positions are free to vary.
column4: Use n rather than n minus one as the free-bit sequence index.~The first value is already x and corresponds to index zero.
